using EpidemicsCFTP, EpidemicsCFTP.abbreviations, EpidemicsUtilities

-----------------

Introduction
============

Overview
--------
We follow @ONeillRoberts-1999 in considering a data set obtained from a smallpox outbreak 
in a closed community of 120
individuals in Abakaliki, Nigeria [see @Bailey-1975, p. 125]. 
We consider only the observed times of subsequent removals (measured in days from first removal).
Of course, while this is an actual dataset, our purpose here is not to deliver a convincing analysis
but rather to show that (at least in principle) the technique of perfect simulation of epidemics
has something to offer.

Setting up parameters for the simulation
----------------------------------------
Removals are separated by the following 
interremoval times (measured in days, but with `0` adjusted to `ε > 0` in order to avoid coincidences).
Specific infectivity and removal rates are defined according to suggestions in @ONeillRoberts-1999
using maximum likelihood analysis by Frank Ball.
```{julia}
#| label: initialization
population     = 120
ε              = 0.001 
interremovals  = [13, 7, 2, 3, ε, ε, 1, 4, 5, 3, 2, ε, 2, ε, 5, 3, 1, 4, ε, 1, 
                   1, 1, 2, ε, 1, 5, ε, 5, 5] 
α, β           = 0.0008, 0.088 
size           = length(interremovals) + 1 
cremoval_times = accumulate(+, interremovals) 
pushfirst!(cremoval_times, 0)
t0             = 0.0
duration       = t0 + maximum(cremoval_times) + 10 ;
```
We emphasize that the first `CRemoval` is deemed to have happened at time `t0=0`.
Plot `duration` is set at `{julia} duration - maximum(cremoval_times)` days after the final removal
(this is a purely photogenic choice).

We create maximal and minimal initial evolutions `evmin0` and `evmax0`, deriving 
respectively from the most
minimal and most maximal initial conditions possible,
under the reasonable assumption that all actual removals have been observed  as `CRemoval`s by time `{julia} duration`,
when our plots end,
(This assumption allows us to speed up the perfect simulation considerably.)
```{julia}
#| label: setting up extremal evolutions
initial     = SIR(0, population - 1, 1, 0)
initial_min = SIR(0, population - 1, 1, 0)
initial_max = SIR(0, population - size, size, 0)

evmin0 = extremal_evolution(initial_min, duration, cremoval_times; 
    maximal=false, size=size, α=α, β=β) ;
evmax0 = extremal_evolution(initial_max, duration, cremoval_times, 
    maximal=true,  size=size, α=α, β=β, all_cremovals_observed=true) ;
```


The random `seed!` is fixed, in order to ensure repeatability.
```{julia}
#| label: initializing random seed
seed!(6) ;
```

Graphical displays of epidemics
-------------------------------
We import some constants from `EpidemicsUtilities`, to be
used for a plotting parameter `select`:
```{julia}
#| label: specific imports from `EpidemicsUtilities`
import EpidemicsUtilities: ACTIVATED, BOUNDARIES, ELEMENTS, LFET, NFZ ;
```

Now we set up graphics and  create a basic `lines_plot` as a basis for subsequent plots. 
```{julia}
#| label: basic graphics settings
theme = create_theme(load_theme("config/animation-theme.yml"))
set_default_plot_size(2theme.figwidth, 0.9theme.figheight)

lines_plot = prepare_screen(initial, evmin0; theme=theme) ;
```

Implementation
==============
We wish to evolve a sequence of `CEvolution`s in algorithmic time, in fact a pair of
such `CEvolution`s, starting at `evmin0` and `evmax0` respectively and using the same 
randomness in an order-preserving way. In particular we are conditioning on `CRemoval`s
being exactly the only `AbstractRemoval`s to be realized, and occurring at the times
listed in `cremoval_times`.
```{julia}
#| label: setup simulation
min_cremovals = [CRemoval(t, n) for (n, t) in enumerate(cremoval_times)]
iv_null       = Innovation(initial.n, Infection[], Removal[], min_cremovals;
                            t0=t0, duration=duration, α=α, β=β, size=size) 
```

We need to consider how many `Infection`s are activated at the initial time `t0=0`.
We assume the first observed removal happens at time zero, and
we need further to assume a Bayesian prior distribution for the numbers of infectives at this time.
Under the assumption that all removals are observed, we know the size of the epidemic
must equal the number of `CRemoval`s plus the initial removal which triggered the data collection
exercise.

One possible prior distribution would be a uniform prior
over the range of possibilities which would not be able to lead to further removals being observed
after the completion of the observation period.
(This means that no removals can take place after the
last `CRemoval` (and therefore that no infectives can occur after the last `CRemoval`!).
This seems unduly pessimistic: in fact under the above assumptions
it is possible to _compute_ a reasonable prior distribution
given α and β.
The argument runs as follows. Assume that there is one index case and that all 
actual removals at _whatever_ time
are observed and are registered as `CRemoval`s. 
In that case one can argue that the relevant distribution 
(which is to say, pertaining to the _unconditioned_ epidemic!) for the
number of infectives at time `0` is the total number who have been infected up to the first actual
removal, less one (the removal!). Now before the initial observation
the relevant process undergoes a sequence of 
infection/removal transitions,
finishing when the first removal occurs. Rates after \(m\) infections (including the index infection),
in a population of size \(n\), are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{infection at rate }& (n-m) m \alpha \\
\text{removal at rate }  &  m \beta
\end{aligned}
\]
and so the chance that the next transition is an infection is 
\[
\frac{(n-m) m \alpha}{(n-m) m \alpha + m \beta}\quad=\quad
\frac{(n-m)\alpha }{(n-m)\alpha + \beta}
\quad=\quad
\frac{1}{1+ \beta/((n-m) \alpha)}\,.
\]
In the particular case being considered, we are dealing with \(n=`{julia} population`\) 
and \(\alpha = `{julia} α`\), \(\beta = `{julia} β`\), so
the chance of the next transition being an infection is (for the first transition)
\[
\frac{1}{1+ \frac{1}{n-1}\frac{\beta}{\alpha}}\quad=\quad
`{julia} 1/(1+ β/((population-1)α))`
\]
and then monotonically decays for further transitions up to the point of the first removal. 
So one can argue that the number of `Infection`s at time `0` is sub-Geometric
(version with smallest value equal to `1`, since we require at least one `Infection` at time zero!)
with this success parameter.
This needs a little more Bayesian justification, based on some 
(perhaps improper?) prior for the (negative) time 
at which the index case is infected, but we omit this for now.

Thus prior probabilities are products of transition probabilities following 
the above theoretical description. @fig-prior-distribution-plot graphs the prior probability mass function.
```{julia}
#| label: prior distribution 
function transition_probability(k)
    return ((population - k) * α) / ((population - k) * α + β)
end
survival = [transition_probability(k) for k in 1:length(min_cremovals)]
priorprob = (1 .- survival) .* pushfirst!(accumulate(*, survival[1:(end-1)]), 1)
push!(priorprob, 1 - sum(priorprob))
iv_ST = InnovationStart_IS(priorprob, 1) ;
```


```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: plot prior pmf 
prior_df = DataFrame(k=1:(1+size), probability=priorprob)
plt = plot(prior_df, x=:k, y=:probability,
    Guide.xlabel("Number of initial infectives", orientation=:horizontal),
    Guide.ylabel("Prior probability", orientation=:vertical),
    Coord.cartesian(xmin=0, xmax=evmin0.size),
    Geom.bar)
draw(PDF("image/prior.pdf"), plt) ;
```

![Prior probability mass function for number of initial infectives in the range `{julia} "1:$size"`.](image/prior.pdf){#fig-prior-distribution-plot}

We need a stream of tuples of `Innovation`s and proposals to change `initial` conditions.
This is supplied by the function `innovation_stream`.
For now we simply ensure this is long enough to fuel the entire CFTP process
up to coalescence,
though in principle it would be easy to extend this as required!
Note that the `size` field in `iv_null` is used to exclude
`Infection`s which if activated would cause the epidemic size to rise above the
specified `size`, while the `α`, `β` and `population` fields determine the intensities of
various kinds of `AbstractIncident`s.
```{julia}
#| label: function `innovation_stream`
import EpidemicsCFTP
function innovation_stream(cycle_length;
            evmin=evmin0, iv_null=iv_null, duration=duration, α=α, β=β, size=size)
    stream, initial = [], evmin0.initial
    for iteration ∈ 1:cycle_length
        push!(stream, (rand(iv_null), rand(iv_ST)))
    end
    return stream
end ;
```

Our update proposes a change in the initial condition
for a `CEvolution`, which will be accepted only if it leads to a valid `CEvolution`.
At present this corresponds to an independence sampler move
though it should be possible to vary this to be a simple Random Walk Metropolis
sampler (_simple RWM_).
In general, care needs to be taken that monotonicity is maintained!
[A similar situation concerning spatial point processes is discussed in @KendallMoeller-2000.]

Using this, 
a function `single_step` updates minimal and maximal `CEvolution`s by a single algorithmic step.
Note that we vary the initial number of infectives using a separate accept/reject step
in the update. Note that here `new_sir` is needed only to supply a proposed initial number
of `Infection`s, though I'd like to deal with `SIR` not `Int`.
```{julia}
#| label: function `single_step`
function single_step(work, evmin, evmax, iv, new_start_proposal; 
        duration=duration, theme=theme)
    evmin = evmin ⋄ iv ▷ new_start_proposal 
    evmax = evmax ⋄ iv ▷ new_start_proposal 

    # Omit next conditional statement once thoroughly tested!
    if !(evmin ⪯ evmax)
        error("Monotonicity fails")
    end

    return evmin, evmax
end ;
```

We need a function to compute the common portions of a minimum and a maximum epidemic trajectory
```{julia}
#| label: function `table_trajectories4`
function table_trajectories4(evmin, evmax, duration)
    # Dataframe holding `evmin` infection points (not including start) as (roughly) `(:t, :xmin == i+r)`
    start_min  = evmin.initial.i + evmin.initial.r
    infect_min = [z for z in evmin.history if z isa AbstractInfection]
    df_min  = DataFrame(t = [z.t for z in infect_min ], xmin = start_min .+ (1:length(infect_min)))
    
    # Dataframe holding `evmax` infection points (not including start) as (roughly) `(:t, :xmax == i+r)`
    start_max  = evmax.initial.i + evmax.initial.r
    infect_max = [z for z in evmax.history if z isa AbstractInfection]
    df_max  = DataFrame(t = [z.t for z in infect_max ], xmax = start_max .+ (1:length(infect_max)))
    
    # Dataframe holding common vertical jumps from `(:t, :x0)` to `(:t, :x1)`
    ysegment = filter(row -> row.xmin==row.xmax, innerjoin(df_min, df_max, on = :t))
    select!(ysegment, :t => :t0, :xmin => (x -> x .- 1) => :x0, :t => :t1, :xmin => :x1)
    
    # Now collect together `df_min` and `df_max` indexed per `t`, 
    # and vertically fill to deal with missing values.
    xsegment = sort(outerjoin(df_min, df_max, on = :t), :t)
    pushfirst!(xsegment, (0, start_min, start_max)) 
    Impute.locf!(xsegment)
    
    # Re-cast into form of possible _starts_ of horizontal jumps, 
    # adding the time from the row below and dropping the row(s) with missing values.
    xsegment = dropmissing(select(xsegment, :t => :t0, :xmin => :x0, 
                                            :t => ShiftedArrays.lead => :t1, :xmax => :x1))
    # Keep only those instances where `x0 == x1`.
    filter!(row -> row.x0 == row.x1, xsegment)
    
    # Return the vertical concatenation of these as the collection of jumps.
    return vcat(xsegment, ysegment)
end ;
```

Most of the work of the CFTP algorithm will be done by the `graphic_cycle!` function.
Note that previous cycles are included in the plots as relevant. Ideally we should plot
these as greyed out, but this is a matter for later.
It is convenient to express the actual drawing in another function
`graphic_component!`.
```{julia}
#| label: function `graphic_component!`
oldblue = range(colorant"white", theme.max, length=3)[2]
oldred  = range(colorant"white", theme.min, length=3)[2]

function graphic_component!(work, evmin, evmax, duration, iteration, stream_length; 
                tag="demo-e", theme=theme, fixed_font="JuliaMono", variable_font="HelveticaBold",
                logo="Minimum and maximum evolutions (using IS at t=0) at algorithmic time step")
    lstream = "-$(lpad(stream_length, 4, "0"))"
    legend = "-$(lpad(stream_length-iteration, 4, "0"))"

    about = "Cycle at time $legend/$lstream"
    info  = Guide.annotation(compose(context(), 
                    font(fixed_font), fontsize(12pt), fill(theme.legend), 
                    text(0.5w, 0.95h, about), fill(theme.legend)))

    if evmin ≃ evmax
        title  = "$logo $legend [COALESCED]"
        signal = Guide.annotation(compose(context(), 
                        font(variable_font), fontsize(24pt), 
                        text(0.5w, 0.8h, "COALESCED"), fill(theme.legend)))
        draw_evolution!(work, evmin, duration, theme=theme, 
                    select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=theme.coalesce, order=4)
        image = new_figure(work, info, signal; title=title)
    else
        title  = "$logo $legend"
        work2 = deepcopy(work)

        merges = layer(table_trajectories4(evmin, evmax, duration),
                           x=:t0, y=:x0, xend=:t1, yend=:x1,
                           Geom.segment, 
                           style(line_width=theme.trail, default_color=theme.joined),
                           order=3)
        push!(work2, merges)
        
        draw_evolution!(work, evmin, duration, theme=theme, 
                    select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=oldred)
        draw_evolution!(work, evmax, duration, theme=theme,
                    select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=oldblue)
       
        draw_evolution!(work2, evmin, duration, theme=theme,
                    select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=theme.min, order=2)
        draw_evolution!(work2, evmax, duration, theme=theme,
                    select=BOUNDARIES, specified_color=theme.max, order=2)
        
        image = new_figure(work2, info; title=title)
    end
                    
    fname   = "animation/$tag-$(lpad(iteration, 4, "0"))"
    draw(PNG("$fname.png"), image)
    if mod(iteration, 10) == 0
        draw(PDF("$fname.pdf"), image)
    end

    return image
end ;                  
```

```{julia}
#| label: function `graphic_cycle!`
function graphic_cycle!(stream, canvas; 
        evmin0=evmin0, evmax0=evmax0, tag="demo-e", lines_plot=lines_plot, 
        fixed_font="JuliaMono", variable_font="HelveticaBold", theme=theme)
    # Create deep copies of plot background and of extremal `CEvolution`s
    evmin, evmax = deepcopy(evmin0), deepcopy(evmax0)
    work = deepcopy(lines_plot)
    stream_length = length(stream)

    image = graphic_component!(work, evmin, evmax, duration, 0, stream_length, tag=tag)
    
    for (iteration, pair) ∈ enumerate(stream)
        (evmin, evmax) = single_step(canvas[iteration], evmin, evmax, pair...)
        image = graphic_component!(canvas[iteration], evmin, evmax,
                                duration, iteration, stream_length, tag=tag)
    end

    draw(PNG("animation/$tag.png"), image)
    draw(PDF("animation/$tag.pdf"), image)
end ;
```

This code is used to plot an entire CFTP sequence of sequences of updates in algorithmic time: see [Appendix @sec-figures].
I suspect that considerable speed-up could be achieved by _not_ plotting each frame of each cycle!

Graphical illustration of CFTP {#sec-figures}
==============================

In this appendix we display an entire evolution of a CFTP run, always starting with minimal and maximal evolutions
`evmin0` and `evmax0` given above. 
An [animated `GIF`](file:///home/wilfrid/ms/PerfectEpidemics/julia/animate.gif) displays the entire CFTP,
evolving in logical time and re-starting earlier and earlier till coalescence is achieved!

The work of each CFTP cycle is carried out by the function `graphic_cycle!`. Note that we have not yet automated 
how CFTP works through cycles.
```{julia}
#| label: building figures
max_length = 256
stream = innovation_stream(max_length)
canvas = [deepcopy(lines_plot) for iteration ∈ 1:max_length]

for (epithet, cycle_length) ∈ [("a", 8), ("b", 16), ("c", 32), ("d", 64), ("e", 128)] 
    graphic_cycle!(stream[max_length - cycle_length + 1:max_length], 
        canvas[max_length - cycle_length + 1:max_length], 
        tag="demo-$epithet")
end
```

Creation of `mp4`
-----------------
1. Use the following to create a sequence of `mp4` movies.
```{bash}
for char in a b c d e ; \
    do ffmpeg -r 12 -i animation/demo-$char-%04d.png -vf scale=258:-1 \
    -vcodec libx264 -crf 25 -pix_fmt yuv420p animation-$char-Y.mp4 ; \
done
```
(Without the `vf` option we get `height not divisible by 2 (576x259)` error here!)

2. This produces a sequence of files `animation-{a,b,c,d,e}-Y.mp4`. 
Add pauses of \(10\) seconds at end of each to form `animation-{a,b,c,d,e}-X.mp4`.
```{bash}
for char in a b c d e ; \
    do ffmpeg -i animation-$char-Y.mp4 \
    -vf tpad=stop_mode=clone:stop_duration=2 animation-$char-X.mp4 ; \
done
```

3. We now need to concatenate
these files:
```{bash}
ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 \
    -i <(for f in ./animation-*-X.mp4; do echo "file '$PWD/$f'"; done) \
    -c copy animation-XX.mp4
```

4. To have a further pause of \(30\) seconds at the end, do
```{bash}
ffmpeg -i animation-XX.mp4 -vf tpad=stop_mode=clone:stop_duration=30 animation.mp4
```

5. Finally clean up intermediate files.
```{bash}
rm -f animation-*.mp4
```

6. [Result is here.](https://wilfridskendall.github.io/talks/PerfectEpidemics/animation/animation.mp4)
